title: Inference: what the evidence allows, and no more
hook: Finish an argument with the conclusion its facts support, and drop the choice that goes too far.

scenes.head: The text
scenes.text: Seed banks store the seeds of crop plants at very low temperatures so that a variety can be replanted if it disappears from farms. Some botanists, however, point out that a stored seed is frozen in time. In the field, a crop's wild relatives keep changing over generations, adapting to new pests and to shifts in climate, but a seed in storage does not. For this reason, these botanists argue that seed banks should be seen as ______
say: An inference question. The blank asks for the conclusion these botanists draw. Read for what the evidence allows, and no more.

scenes.prompt: Predict how the blank ends, in your own words.
say: Before you look at any choices, read it again and predict the ending yourself. Take as long as you need, then continue.

scenes.head: Read it like the test-writer
scenes.text: Seed banks store seeds {{so that a variety can be replanted if it disappears|ok|what they do well}}. However, {{a stored seed is frozen in time|bad|the limit}}: wild relatives {{keep changing over generations|brand|what storage misses}}, adapting to new pests and climate. So seed banks should be seen as ______
say: Mark what the text says seed banks do well. They let a lost variety be replanted.
Then the turn. However: a stored seed is frozen in time.
Here's what storage misses. Plants in the field keep adapting.
So the conclusion has to keep both facts. Seed banks help, and they have a limit.

scenes.head: The plan
items: seed banks help (replanting) AND have a limit (no adapting)
the choice that keeps both, and nothing stronger
say: Keep both facts in mind: they help, and they have a limit.
A good prediction: a backup with a limit.
Then match. The right choice says both things and nothing stronger.

scenes.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a replacement for protecting crops' wild relatives where they grow.
a useful backup that cannot, on its own, keep pace with the adapting that happens in the field.
unnecessary, since crops in the field continue to adapt without them.
the main reason that modern crops resist new pests.
notes: Reverses it: stored seeds do NOT keep adapting, so they cannot replace plants in the field.
Keeps both facts: a backup, with a limit.
Too extreme: a limit is not the same as useless.
Goes beyond the text: it never credits seed banks for pest resistance.
say: Here are the choices. Check each one against both facts.
C is the trap. The text does criticize seed banks, so unnecessary feels right. But a limit isn't the same as useless.
A turns the argument around. Stored seeds can't replace plants that keep adapting.
D goes beyond the text. Pest resistance comes from the field, not the bank.
B keeps both facts: a useful backup, with a limit. That's the answer.
scenes.passage: Seed banks store the seeds of crop plants at very low temperatures so that a variety can be replanted if it disappears from farms. Some botanists, however, point out that a stored seed is frozen in time. In the field, a crop's wild relatives keep changing over generations, adapting to new pests and to shifts in climate, but a seed in storage does not. For this reason, these botanists argue that seed banks should be seen as ______

scenes.head: The trap
scenes.bad: The text criticizes seed banks, so they must be unnecessary.
scenes.good: A limit is not a rejection. The text still says seed banks let a lost variety be replanted.
say: The trap is reading criticism as rejection.
The botanists name a limit. They never say seed banks are useless, and the text says they let a lost variety be replanted.

points: When you see an inference blank, think: the conclusion must keep every fact in the text, and nothing stronger.
